summary: Defines the standard way to express SNMP Structure of Management Information base datatypes in XML Schema Definition language, so XML documents can match the SMI as faithfully as possible. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Translating the labels used for network device data into another language, XML, keeping the meaning the same.

questions: how to represent snmp datatypes in xml
why does octet string use hexbinary in xsd
subtitle: The standard way to write SNMP's base data types in XML Schema, so management data looks the same in every XML tool.

tldr.problem: Several independent schemes existed for expressing SNMP SMI datatypes in XML Schema Definition (XSD), and they differed enough, especially for non-numeric types, to prevent interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines one XSD schema that maps each SMIv2 base datatype to an XSD datatype: numeric types to XSD integer types, OCTET STRING and Opaque to hexBinary, and IpAddress and OBJECT IDENTIFIER to pattern-restricted strings.
tldr.outcome: XML documents can faithfully carry SMI values and be validated with XSD. It covers base datatypes only; textual conventions and MIB structure were left for planned future memos.

today: RFC 5935 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers base datatypes only; the RFC says memos for textual conventions and MIB structure were planned but not yet produced at the time of writing.

sections.title: Why SMI Needs an XML Mapping
sections.content:
MIB modules describe management data using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). SMIv2 is defined in RFC 2578, and legacy modules used SMIv1 from RFC 1155. Values in SNMP messages use the primitive base datatypes the SMI defines. Many XML-based management applications want to reuse that data, or reach SNMP agents through gateways.

The RFC says various independent schemes had been devised for expressing SMI datatypes in XSD. They agreed on numeric types but differed on the non-numeric ones, which blocked uniformity and interoperability. This memo is the single IETF standard expression.

Values of objects defined with a textual convention (RFC 2579) are always encoded as the base datatype underneath, so the mappings cover those objects too. The RFC explicitly does not redesign SMIv2 datatypes or fix their known limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: People had made several different translation guides from network-device labels into XML, and they did not match. This memo picks one guide for everybody.

sections.title: The Seven Requirements
sections.content:
The memo lists requirements R1 to R7 for the mapping:

  • R1: every SMI base datatype MUST have a corresponding XSD datatype.
  • R2: SMIv2 is normative; legacy SMIv1 modules MUST first be converted, at least logically, as in Section 2.1 of RFC 3584.
  • R3: the XSD type MUST be able to represent all valid values.
  • R4: it MUST represent any special encoding rules.
  • R5: it MUST include any value restrictions.
  • R6: it MUST be the most logical XSD type with the fewest necessary restrictions.
  • R7: the XML output SHOULD be coherent and succinct, avoiding superfluous decoration, for human readability.

Together these aim at fidelity: accurate, consistent representation of SMI values as they appear on the wire in SNMP PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say the translation must never lose or change anything, must pick the simplest fitting XML type, and should be easy for people to read.

sections.title: The Schema and the Base Datatypes
sections.content:
The schema covers the eleven SMIv2 ObjectSyntax base datatypes of RFC 2578: INTEGER, Integer32, Unsigned32, Gauge32, Counter32, TimeTicks, Counter64, OCTET STRING, Opaque, IpAddress and OBJECT IDENTIFIER. The BITS pseudo-type is treated as a textual convention, not a base datatype.

The schema lives in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:smi:base:1.0 and defines each type as an XSD simpleType. The numeric mappings are plain restrictions of XSD built-ins with no extra rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives a translation table with one XML type for each kind of network-device value, written as a short, machine-checkable file.

sections.title: How Each Type Is Mapped
sections.content:
Numbers. INTEGER and Integer32 map to xs:int. Unsigned32, Gauge32, Counter32 and TimeTicks map to xs:unsignedInt. Counter64 maps to xs:unsignedLong. Canonical forms have no leading plus sign and no leading zeros. Gauge32, Counter32, Counter64 and TimeTicks have special application semantics, described in RFC 2578, which matter when the raw value is used for more than display or storage.

OCTET STRING and Opaque. Both map to xs:hexBinary, with each octet as two hexadecimal digits (0-9 and uppercase A-F in canonical form). The RFC rejects xs:string because it cannot faithfully represent every octet value (0 through 255) readably. OCTET STRING also gets a maxLength of 65535 octets.

IpAddress. It is an xs:string restricted by a pattern to dotted decimal: four values from 0 to 255 separated by periods, with no leading zeros. IPv6 is out of scope because the SMI uses textual conventions for it.

ObjectIdentifier. It is also a pattern-restricted xs:string, a dotted-decimal list of up to 128 sub-ids, each an Unsigned32 value. The first two components have limited ranges. The minimum is two sub-ids, so the zero value is 0.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting numbers become normal XML numbers. Raw bytes are spelled out in two-letter codes so nothing gets lost. Addresses and long dotted numbers are written as text that has to follow a strict pattern.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The mapping itself introduces no new security considerations; the considerations of any given MIB module still apply to its XML form. The RFC warns that if proxies or gateways later carry SNMP data to XML applications, care will be needed to support all applicable SNMP security mechanisms in a manner yet to be determined.

Following RFC 3688, the IANA XML registry was updated with the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:smi:base:1.0 and a schema registration, both with the IESG as contact.
sections.plainLanguage: Translating the labels does not add new dangers, but anyone building a bridge between the two systems must still keep the existing safety rules.
